start.text: Hi! I'm Dr. Ahmed Aziz Ezzat, an Industrial and Systems Engineering professor here at Rutgers. My work brings together data science, AI, and engineering decision-making.

challenge.text: Let me ask you something: if you could turn an idea into a physical part, how would you know whether the process was actually working well?

research.text: I work on data-driven problems involving forecasting, quality, and reliability, including energy and industrial systems. The interesting part is turning data into better decisions.

choices.label: How does that connect to this printer?

reliability.text: Reliability asks whether a system performs as expected over time. Even a sophisticated machine is only useful if you can depend on its results.

choices.label: How would you check that here?

printer.text: This is the Bambu Lab X1E. It takes a digital design and builds a physical object one layer at a time using filament.

measure_intro.text: Good question. You could track how often a print succeeds, how long it takes, and how much material it uses. One successful print doesn't tell the whole story.

prototype.text: A prototype lets you test an idea before committing to a final design. Sometimes the most useful result is discovering what needs to change.

choices.label: What would an ISE student test?

ams_intro.text: The X1E can work with an Automatic Material System, or AMS. It manages loaded filament spools and can switch between compatible filaments during a print.

choices.label: How does this relate to ISE?

ams.text: It gives designers more flexibility with colors and compatible materials. But remember: more options also mean more decisions about settings, cost, and quality.

choices.label: How would you make those decisions?

ise.text: ISE students don't just ask, 'Can we make the part?' They also ask, 'Can we make it consistently, efficiently, and with less waste?'

choices.label: How would you improve the process?

optimization.text: Suppose two print settings produce acceptable parts, but one is faster and the other uses less material. Which would you choose? It depends on what matters most.

tradeoffs.text: That's an engineering tradeoff. You could compare print time, material cost, quality, and the chance of failure before choosing a process.

metrics.text: I would start with data: print time, material consumption, dimensional accuracy, and failure rate. Once you measure a process, you can start to improve it.

failure.text: A failed print is information, not just wasted material. Look for patterns: was there a setting change, a material issue, or something else worth investigating?

choices.label: How do we find a pattern?

variation.text: Two prints made from the same design may not be identical. Engineers study that variation to understand whether the process is stable and what affects quality.

ai.text: With enough useful data, AI and statistical models may help identify patterns or flag possible failures. But a model still needs good measurements and engineering judgment.

choices.label: So AI doesn't replace the engineer?
How does this help ISE students?

judgment.text: Exactly. Data gives you evidence; engineering helps you ask the right question and decide what to do with the answer. Don't stop at the first result.

choices.label: How would a student apply that?

student.text: A student might print a bracket, test its fit, revise the CAD design, and repeat. Then they could compare each version for quality, time, and material use.

choices.label: Could you explain process improvement again?

closing.text: Here's my challenge to you: don't just admire a machine because it works. Ask how you'd measure its performance, why it sometimes fails, and what you'd improve next.

finish.text: Keep asking those questions wherever you go in the lab. That's how we turn an interesting technology into a better engineering system. Enjoy exploring!

bye.text: Of course! Feel free to come back if another question comes to mind. Enjoy exploring the room.
